text.p: The following are the main stories from Thursday morning's Austrian newspapers:

- The justice committee passed a law on new investigation methods with the approval of the government. By autumn systematic searches will be introduced and from next summer a bugging offensive begins, from which even lawyers will not be exempt.

- Pressure continues on Foreign Minister Wolfgang Schuessel despite a meeting with Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer over allegations he called him a "real pig". Voices from coalition partners the Social Democrats are now joining opposition calls for his resignation.
- Michael Jackson gave a concert in Vienna on Wednesday.
- The fusion of the investment banks of Creditanstalt and Bank Austria will take place this autumn.
- A consortium consisting of Creditanstalt Investmentbank and British mobile phone firm Orange will challenge the existing bidder, the Connect-Austria consortium, for the third mobile phone licence.
- Interior Minister Karl Schloegl said the border with Italy should not be opened in one step and conceded the possibility of a "half-open" border with Germany by the end of the year.
- Social Minister Lore Hostasch insists pension reforms must be in place by September.
- Steelmaker VA Stahl is in talks with several companies in Eastern Europe over a possible takeover after a planned merger with Czech rival Nova Hut fell through.
- Economic research institute Wifo cites a dramatic increase in the number of older people out of work, but says that without early retirement the situation on the job market would be much worse.

- The battle over the planned sale of a 25 percent stake in Upper Austrian energy plant OKA is escalating. Regional electricity firm EVN, Verbund, Wiener Stadtwerke and Energieholding Steiermark are all bidding for the stake.
- Cheap jobs are too expensive for the market. The rate of joblessness is on the rise.
- Women should be allowed to retire later. One of the planned pension reforms is to raise the age of retirement for women to 65.
- A technology drive launched by the government in June should bring in valuable jobs to the market.

- Austrians are proud of their country and believe they live better here than in other European Union countries, a survey showed. They said medical care, a clean environment and social security were among the main advantages.
